reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A rare malignant soft-tissue sarcoma with epithelioid morphology and a notorious tendency to be mistaken for a benign process
The classic distal form arises in the hands, forearms and feet of young adults, often as a slow-growing nodule that may ulcerate and mimic a non-healing wound or granuloma
The proximal-type variant occurs in the pelvis, perineum and trunk of older patients and behaves more aggressively
Characterised by loss of nuclear SMARCB1 (INI1) expression on immunohistochemistry in the large majority of cases
Histology shows nodules of epithelioid and spindled cells with central necrosis, sometimes creating a granuloma-like appearance
Tumour cells co-express epithelial markers (cytokeratin, EMA) and CD34, an unusual combination that aids diagnosis
It spreads along fascial planes and via lymphatics, with a high rate of local recurrence and regional nodal and distant metastasis
reference.pathophysiology: Epithelioid sarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumour defined in most cases by inactivation of the SMARCB1 (INI1) tumour suppressor gene, a core subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex. Loss of SMARCB1 function disrupts normal chromatin regulation and gene expression, promoting oncogenesis, and is detected as loss of nuclear INI1 staining. The tumour grows as nodules of epithelioid cells that frequently undergo central necrosis, producing a deceptively granuloma-like or necrobiotic pattern. It characteristically infiltrates along tendons, fascia and nerves and has a marked propensity for lymph node involvement, which is unusual among sarcomas.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatous inflammation such as a rheumatoid nodule or granuloma annulare
Fibrous histiocytoma or other benign nodule
additionalInvestigations: MRI to define the primary extent and infiltration along fascial planes
Biopsy with histological assessment of necrotising epithelioid nodules
Immunohistochemistry showing co-expression of cytokeratin, EMA and CD34
INI1 (SMARCB1) immunostaining to demonstrate loss of nuclear expression
Nodal and distant staging given the propensity for lymphatic and haematogenous spread
redFlags: A non-healing ulcer or persistent nodule on the hand or forearm not responding to expected treatment
Proximal-type tumour of the pelvis or perineum, which is more aggressive
Local recurrence or distant metastasis during follow-up
reference.prognosis: Epithelioid sarcoma is an aggressive malignancy prone to local recurrence and to regional nodal and distant metastasis, and it often follows a protracted but ultimately unfavourable course. The proximal-type variant, large size and metastatic disease at presentation carry a worse prognosis.
pitfalls: Mistaking a necrotising nodule for benign granulomatous disease and delaying diagnosis
Interpreting keratin positivity as evidence of carcinoma rather than epithelioid sarcoma
Failing to perform INI1 staining, which typically shows diagnostic loss
Neglecting nodal staging given the unusual lymphatic spread of this sarcoma
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Manage at, or in close consultation with, a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary centre from diagnosis.
For localized disease, wide local excision with clear margins is the mainstay; extensive resection is often needed given spread along fascia, tendons and nerves.
Consider adjuvant radiotherapy after limb-sparing surgery to reduce local recurrence risk, especially with close margins or deep tumors.
Reserve amputation for extensive distal disease where margin-negative limb-sparing surgery is not achievable.

Assess regional nodal basins clinically and radiologically given the meaningful risk of nodal metastasis; biopsy grossly involved nodes and consider complete lymph node dissection if nodal disease is confirmed without distant metastasis.
Counsel that proximal-type disease behaves more aggressively and is more resistant to radiotherapy and chemotherapy than distal-type disease.
For unresectable or metastatic disease, consider an anthracycline-based systemic regimen, recognizing responses are typically modest and short-lived.
Test for INI1/SMARCB1 loss when the diagnosis is suspected; if confirmed, an EZH2 inhibitor (tazemetostat) is a genotype-directed option for unresectable or metastatic disease.
Treat combined EZH2 inhibitor plus anthracycline therapy as investigational, outside a clinical trial, pending confirmatory frontline study results.
Refer patients with locally advanced or metastatic disease for clinical trial enrollment, ideally at a sarcoma referral center.
Provide prolonged surveillance with cross-sectional imaging of the primary site, regional nodes, and chest well beyond the first few years, given ongoing risk of local and distant recurrence.
Promptly re-biopsy or image any new nodule, non-healing lesion, or regional lymphadenopathy during follow-up.
Refer for confirmatory INI1 (SMARCB1) immunohistochemistry or molecular testing whenever the diagnosis is suspected.
Refer to medical oncology, ideally with sarcoma trial access, for unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic disease.
